questions.question: What is the relationship between an image and a container?
options: A container is a running instance of an immutable image, plus a writable layer
An image is a running container that was paused
questions.explanation: The image is the immutable, layered template; each container instantiates it with its own thin writable layer on top. Think class vs object.

questions.question: In `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx`, what does 8080:80 mean?
questions.explanation: The format is HOST:CONTAINER. Traffic hitting the host on 8080 is forwarded to port 80 inside the container. Getting this backwards is the most common port-mapping bug.

questions.question: How do containers differ fundamentally from virtual machines?
options: Containers virtualize hardware; VMs virtualize the OS
Containers share the host kernel via namespaces/cgroups; VMs each run their own kernel on a hypervisor
There is no difference in isolation model
questions.explanation: Containers are isolated processes on a shared kernel (namespaces limit visibility, cgroups limit resources), so they start in milliseconds. VMs boot a full guest OS on virtualized hardware — stronger isolation, heavier cost.

questions.question: Why should `COPY package*.json ./` + `RUN npm ci` come before `COPY . .` in a Dockerfile?
options: Layer caching: dependencies reinstall only when manifests change, not on every source edit
questions.explanation: Docker caches layers top-down and invalidates from the first changed layer. Copying only the manifests first means source-code edits don't bust the expensive dependency-install layer — rebuilds go from minutes to seconds.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a multi-stage build?
options: Run multiple apps in one container
Build with heavy toolchains but ship a final image containing only the runtime artifacts
questions.explanation: Earlier stages can use full SDK images (compilers, dev deps); the final stage COPY --from's just the built artifacts onto a slim base. Result: dramatically smaller images and less attack surface. (Multi-arch is buildx, a different feature.)

questions.question: A container exits with code 137. What does that usually indicate?
options: The process received SIGKILL — typically the OOM killer hit a memory limit
questions.explanation: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). In containers that almost always means the kernel's OOM killer terminated the process for exceeding its memory limit. Check `docker inspect` (OOMKilled: true) and `docker stats`.

questions.question: Data written inside a container's filesystem survives `docker rm` of that container.
questions.explanation: False. The writable layer is deleted with the container. Persistent data must live in a volume or bind mount — which is exactly why databases in Compose files always declare volumes.

questions.question: On a user-defined Docker network, containers can reach each other by container name via built-in DNS.
questions.explanation: True. User-defined networks include a DNS server that resolves container (and Compose service) names, e.g. `db:5432`. The legacy default bridge network does NOT provide name resolution — a classic gotcha.

questions.question: Your CI builds take 8 minutes; profiling shows npm install runs on every build even for README-only changes. What's the fix?
options: Reorder the Dockerfile so dependency manifests are copied and installed before the full source COPY
questions.explanation: The layer cache is being invalidated by `COPY . .` placed before the install. Copy package*.json, install, then copy the rest — README changes then reuse the cached install layer.

questions.question: Security review flags that your app container runs as root. What's the standard Dockerfile remediation?
options: Add `USER <non-root>` after setup steps (creating the user if the base image lacks one)
questions.explanation: Create/switch to an unprivileged user with the USER instruction so the app process isn't root even if the container is compromised. (privileged: false is already the default; it doesn't change the in-container user.)

questions.question: Write the command to list ALL containers, including stopped ones.
questions.explanation: `docker ps` shows only running containers; -a/--all includes exited ones — essential when debugging a container that crashed at startup.

questions.question: Write the command to open an interactive bash shell in the running container named `api`.
questions.explanation: exec runs a new process in a running container; -i keeps stdin open and -t allocates a TTY, which together give you a usable shell.

questions.question: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
options: CMD runs at build time; ENTRYPOINT at run time
ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD supplies default arguments that `docker run` arguments replace
They are interchangeable in all cases
questions.explanation: With both set, the container runs ENTRYPOINT + CMD. Arguments after `docker run image ...` override CMD but not ENTRYPOINT (unless --entrypoint). Pattern: ENTRYPOINT ["myapp"], CMD ["--default-flag"].

questions.question: Using the `latest` tag for base images in production Dockerfiles is recommended because you always get security fixes automatically.
questions.explanation: False. `latest` makes builds non-reproducible — the same Dockerfile can produce different images on different days and break without any code change. Pin versions (ideally digests) and upgrade deliberately via automated PRs (Renovate/Dependabot).

questions.question: In Docker Compose, what does `depends_on` guarantee by default?
options: The dependency is started first AND ready to accept connections
Only start order — the dependency's container starts first, but readiness isn't checked
questions.explanation: Plain depends_on orders startup only; Postgres may still be initializing when your app connects. Use `condition: service_healthy` with a healthcheck, or make the app retry connections.
